Yes exactly. Not applicable to all light roasts but natural and anaerobic fermentation processes can introduce very easily over-extractable acids and bitter components. It’s just a by product of bacterial breakdown of the sugars in the berry fruit.
If it makes you salivate it’s traditional sour. If it leaves your mouth dry it’s over extracted.

So ideally to dial in a bean you should stay with the same profile until you can get a somewhat palatable shot. That’s why the Decent has a “Default profile” basically a 9 bar shot with PI. Thats when you have a grind setting you have your starting reference point. Is the drink too harsh? Maybe you need a less intense extraction profile. Need more from the bean? You can grind finer with a profile that has a longer PI.

It is my personal preference to start pulling shots at 93c and increasing or decreasing temps based on what I’m getting from there. I’ll dial in my grind to approximate the flow that I want. Then I adjust temps based on taste. Higher temps will get more sour and more bitter if the flavor is flat. I’ll lower the temps if there’s too many harsh flavors like bitter pith
Your grind size, while exposing more surface area, will be the primary determinant on how difficult it is for water to pass through the puck
Temperature and pressure determine a lot about how much solubles you get in the final cup and what soluble you get

So for anyone following my journey with Blackstrap from Irving Farms:
My last 6 bar shot at 84 was getting really close to the notes on the bag. Still had some ever so slight bright mouth drying notes. 
Today I tried an Adaptive for Light roasts profile at 85 degrees with a slightly finer grind (one click) as this has a lengthy pre-infusion. Darker flavor on the finish but I would like a little more of that darker caramelized molasses flavor. So for the next shot I would bump up the temp by 3 degrees and see how that runs. Overall the 6 bar flat shot and this shot are very tasty and I would serve these to family memebers and friends. Now its just fine tuning. Overall took 6 shots to get here from what the roaster recommends (and I started from a 9 bar shot which I wouldn't normally do given the lightness of the roast) but if you're using a single basket it is a total of 48 grams of the 300 in the bag. It's definitely not about hitting 9 bar. I would watch more of his videos on the topic for clarification. The benefits of stepdown that I'm aware of are that coarser grinds means more even extraction, and deeper bed means better filtration of astringent particles. At any given pressure target, the flow rate is also more stable throughout the shot compared to a thinner bed, which I assume is also why you're getting similarly high extraction despite coarser grind (longer contact time?). If you ground at the similar level of coarseness for a 58mm, you would get much higher flow rates and lower contact time, so I'm doubtful that you would achieve a similar level of extraction.
From this you want to be tweaking by taste.
Everything else is just numbers

But if you're using a darker roast you don't necessarily want to go to the 3:1 ratio. As long as you're hitting the flow target with some reasonable pressure (anecdotally I like 6-7 peak with my current beans) you're pretty much within the profile intent, so use your taste buds to guide any tweaks

3 main parts of phase profiling: Targets, Limits, and Stop Conditions

Target - flow or pressure you're aiming for
Limit - flow or pressure (opposite of target) that you don't go over

Light and bright flavors need delicate extractions (something under 6 bar either turbo style, something with a longer PI and bloom etc.) I prefer lower temps for these (under 90c). Coffees medium or dark that start the tasting notes with chocolate or toffee or caramel would benefit from a 9 bar shot like londinium, cremina, leva 9. Temps 90 and above with well here

In july flimsybeets recommended 85 degrees. Point is temperature is far less dogmatic than what people are claiming it to be. I have had great coferments at 80 degrees and wonderful Ethiopians at 85 and columbian italian roasts at 92. Each bean is different and I found a relatively harsh and easily extracted bean does well with colder temps
Any time I have a harsh bean I go with a high flow low pressure low temp profile which tends to bring out juicier and clearer flavors.

I also tend to find that mouthfeel descriptors tend to more accurately descibe what is happening in the cup than sour/bitter. There are a lot of acids in coffee that can be sour and bitter and feeling if it is drying in the mouth vs making you salivate can be a really helpful indicator whether you need to extract more (hotter) or less (colder). Many natural washed Ethiopians I have found are drying the tounge at 90 degrees with a harsh flavor.
That also assumes the puck passes the nickel test and the water and machine is adequately heated for 15 mins.

The goal is to get the whole  group and surrounding machine housing  plus pf up to temp, it's basically reaching a equilibrium, the heat dissipation of the metal is high but so are the losses, by keeping the machine temperature at steam you might just slightly improve the heatup time but it's going to have a negative toll on the heating elements and other boiler attached components like gaskets and so, all this for a 3 minutes difference is not worth it imo.

Predictive scales aren't real scales, it's basically software trying to guess based on a set of rules and sensors readings when coffee has started falling into the cup, because it's not magic it can't be perfect so yeah in many complex cases taring once you see first drips hitting the cup will make the predicted output as close as possible to reality

A caveat to what zer0 said is,  If the predictive scale thinks coffee is in the cup and starts counting weight early it's possible to skip phases prematurely. So if you were to only hit the tare button on first drops you may have already skipped phases.   Hence Srals suggestion of taring like mad aka continuously hitting the tare button until espresso has reached the cup to prevent premature phase changes on profile phases with a weight stop condition. 

Personally (I use predictive scales currently) I usually disable weight conditions on profile phases that cause me issues frequently. Like blooming

During a shot, the only mechanism the system has to control pressure is the flow (the pump). For any phase of a profile is either flow based or pressure based. Otherwise I usually go with the question „which curve is more complicated“ or the opposite „which curve looks like a straight limit“.  Example is IUIUIU, where the pressure is the target and you dial flow by taste. Here's a quick summary of profiling with Gaggiuino: 
A profile is a recipe for extracting coffee, and is typically designed for a specific amount of grounds. When the grind is "dialed in" the graphed pressure and flow will follow a general target shape.,Profiles are made up of phases. Each phase has a target (either flow or pressure) and may have a limit (the other). There are also phase stop conditions (time, weight, volume pumped, pressure) that can stop the phase, starting the next one. For example, it's common to have a weight and/or pressure condition to exit soak, e.g. move to next phase if >1g in the cup or pressure <1 bar or time of 30sec.,Profiles have a "dial-to-taste" range where the pressure and flow on the graph match the profile intent and further adjustments need taste bud data. At that point dialing is done with slight grind and volume/ratio adjustments based on sour/bitter/dry/sweet/thin/thick taste preferences.,Profile descriptions can be found in Community Profiles in the Gaggiuino WebUI as well as in the ⁠profiles channel. 
If you have a shot you'd like help dialing in, post a picture of the graph here in ⁠dialing-n-profiling.
For general info about profiling, see https://espressoaf.com/guides/profiling.html (editado)domingo, 1 de febrero de 2026, 21:24

Yes grind size, ratio, and temperature would be the main things you can change while using the same profile.  Time is a dependent variable when you have a machine capable of profiling. With Gaggiuino you can see exactly what you did wrong (too high or low, pressure or flow) so time is basically irrelevant. Weight flow is just a result of a live extraction that would validate how accurate the pump control is

But isn't pump flow different from weight flow? If there is no resistance (i.e. no portafilter in the group head), pump flow should be equal to weight flow. But if the water has to pass through the coffee bed, the weight flow should be lower than the pump flow or am I missing something?

Pump flow is formula based calculation of the flow based on pump cycles, weight flow is the flow calculated based on liquid hitting the scales, conceptually they both should align as they target the same resulting idea but the implementation is different because one allows for proactive control while the other is more of a nice to have  validation

So to answer your question once extraction starts weight flow should always align with pump flow or be as close as possible since perfect alignment is impossible ofc since one is proactive and the other is reactive (editado)miércoles, 28 de enero de 2026, 11:40

@thlp0110 it is expected that the initial PZ calibration won't be perfect. There is tolerance in brand new pumps and the flow rate at 0 pressure is not the same between every pump.  So when you move to real shots with pressure you will need to adjust PZ.
Different profiles may react slightly different to PZ but overall once you find your correct PZ it should be close enough for most standard profiles. 

Stop on weight is how predictive stops the shot. If you disable it you will have to manually stop the shot. This is helpful when you are still dialing in the PZ value when running real shots. But once you get it set you can start using it. 

Things to keep in mind
You must hit the tare button on first drops for accurate predicted weight. Every shot, no exceptions. 

Fast flow profiles like a turbo profile are very hard for predictive to get right because the timing of the tare needs to be exact and if you are a second off you are now 5 grams behind. So it's usually better to manually stop those shits while using a scale. 

If you need more help post in your help thread, or start one.
